predictions.text: Why does Jennifer/Mary Sue decide to stay at the end of Pleasantville? At the end of Pleasantville , David's sister Jennifer/Mary Sue rather abruptly decides she'd rather stay there than go back to their "real" life. Why? It feels super out of character to me. She is the one to resent Pleasantville most in the beginning, and aside from discovering a love for reading (which she could pursue just the same in the real world), she isn't shown to develop genuine feelings for anyone in P., or otherwise have a change of mind. When she and David separate, she gives her reason as "I have more of a chance to go to college here" (or something along that line), which sounds extremely lame, considering she never before bothered much about her education. That a modern (though superficial) woman like Jennifer would be willing to stay in a world like Pleasantville with its limited options for women, leaving her family in return (to which she does appear to be attached), does seem OOC. (Not to mention the difficulties David and their mother would have to explain the sudden disappearance of Jennifer in the real world.) It smells like for some reason the authors had to have only one of the two come back to the present, but I don't understand the reason why. Is there an explanation out there?

How many characters in Legends (2026) were actually real people? Legends (2026) is a TV series about undercover customs agents infiltrating drug gangs in 1990s England, which is mostly based on a true story , but how many of the characters are real people who actually existed in this operation? It's well documented that Guy Stanton really does exist , and that Mylonas is also closely based on a real person (Keravnos, a Greek Cypriot casino owner turned police informant), and also Afridi was a real person , while Guy's wife really was a fellow customs agent although her name isn't Sophie. What about other characters: Don, Kate, Bailey, Erin - were the other members of the team also real people, or fictionalised versions of people who worked with Guy Stanton? Hakan, Aziz, Carter, Eddie - were any of these real drug lords who got caught, or just characters created for the TV series? Was Keravnos's wife really an Afghan princess, or was that invented for the TV series?

Why isn't Bruce Willis's character in the Sixth Sense self-aware? Why doesn't Bruce Willis's character realize he is dead? If I remember correctly, the plot takes place several months after he is killed. Shouldn't there have been some clues during that time? They do imply that he thinks his wife isn't speaking to him because she's angry, but is it really possible that she was the only person he expected to interact with? Additionally, it seems that all the other ghosts in the movie know they're dead. So perhaps another question would be do all ghosts in The Sixth Sense go through a "transition period" where they don't realize they're dead? At what point to they become aware of it?

Even after the Bishop fires his pistol at V, why does the government spy do nothing, and just snicker, until Bishop wails "I don't want to die"? I am at my wits' end with . From his surveillance truck, this government spy has been actively eavesdropping on the heated exchange between V, and Bishop Anthony Lilliman. Part of the audio surveillance division (the "Ear") , this spy must have heard Lilliman shooting his sidearm, hidden in his Bible, at V! But the film shows the spy just listening and chortling, until Lilliman desperately squeals — LILLIMAN: I don't want to die! Only upon hearing this, does the spy finally report this exchange as an emergency, of course too late for the police to save the Bishop. Why didn't the spy log this confrontation much earlier, like when Lilliman discharges his handgun? And what was this spy sniggling at? V and Lilliman weren't kidding around. I don't find any comedy in the showdown between V and Lilliman?

Did the Pope intend Cardinal Lawrence to break into his room and find the report on Tremblay? In the movie Conclave it is made clear that the Pope was "eight moves ahead" (in the words of Cardinal Bellini) and laid traps for e.g. Adeyemi and Tremblay. For instance, Tremblay's involvement in recruiting Sister Shanumi evidently sheds a negative light on him, as discussed in this question . However, what ultimately brings down Cardinal Tremblay is the report on his corruption that Lawrence finds hidden in the late Pope's headboard, after breaking into his (sealed) rooms and which he then shares with the college of cardinals. Note that this answer assesses that the Pope's plan is "fairly flimsy and contrived" and I concur. Am I right in thinking that the Pope couldn't possibly have foreseen that Lawrence a) breaks into his room and then b) finds the report without even knowing about it? Did the Pope hope that the Shanumi affair alone would suffice in preventing his papacy? EDIT: Upon closer examination it seems that a combination of both ends Tremblay's candidacy, since Sister Agnes confirms that he brought Sister Shanumi to the conclave. After this revelation, Adeyemi accuses him of treason and leaves the room. However, the distribution of the reports still seems to play a decisive role.

What rules govern how TV show opening credits are structured? I've always been curious what decides if a credit is in the opening or closing credits. It seems loosely that cast (in order of today's "big name" significance), directors and financiers get the front spots, and everything else appears later. But lately I've been developing some specific curiosities about how cast members are credited on TV shows. Opening credits seem to follow this rough outline: Part of "opening credits" video segment (optional) Major Actors Show Title Core Cast Actors Directors Producers (optional) Episode Title Episode Writers Subtitles over beginning of show, after opening video (Episode Title and Writers may appear here, instead) Special Guest Actors I've probably missed a few things, and mis-ordered a few things. But, as I said, my main curiosity is about actor credits. Typically, there is little indication of which characters the core cast actors play. Sometimes their name is edited to appear along with an image of the character as an indictator, but sometimes there is no indication. As I've never seen anyone credited in both the opening and closing credits, that leaves the potential for core actors to never be directly associated with their character. This seems potentially problematic; is there a reason for this? Are viewers expected to know who's who? Guest actors sometimes are simply credited by name (and not being part of the opening video, this means they will never be associated with their character in credits). But often they are credited as " special guest as character name ". This is quite helpful. The thing I find really confusing is, sometimes the last few regular cast actors will get the guest actor treatment. I've seen opening video with "and actor as character " paired with an image of that character for an entire season. Why does this actor get special treatment? Finally, sometimes guest actors will be credited at the front following the opening video, sometimes they'll be credited in the closing credits. Are there rules for deciding who get's credited early or late? I've sometimes wondered if shows deliberately play with actor's name position to obfuscate plot arcs ("you won't think we're killing of this character if their actor is still in the opening credits", or "you won't expect this recurring guest if we place their name in the closing credits") and I've also wondered if there are thresholds for "people appearing in XX number or YY percentage of episodes get placed here ." But it's difficult to build a good sampling base for this. And season 7 of Stargate SG-1 kinda took a shotgun to my guesses so far. So... Are there rules?

Both the husband and wife were Caucasian, I think middle-class. They were traveling for their honeymoon and they had a camper, either as a vehicle or as a trailer, and the wife kept picking up (rather large) rocks from the places they stopped at as a keepsake, something which frustrated her new husband, who I think had to haul them into the camper. At a later point in the film, they're driving up a hill, and the vehicle is failing, forcing them to jettison the rocks one by one to lighten the load. I think it leads to them arguing (details I don't recall, but probably something along the lines of that he didn't understand why she was collecting rocks and she didn't know why he didn't understand the sentimental values of the rocks), with them eventually reconciling and being more in love by the end of the film.

Why does Scarecrow in The Wizard Of Oz get the Pythagorean Theorem wrong? After receiving a "brain," the Scarecrow in The Wizard of Oz famously says the following : “The sum of the square roots of any two sides of an isosceles triangle is equal to the square root of the remaining side!” Which as generations of know-it-alls have noted, is incorrect. That's a right triangle, you idiot! Over the years I have a number of conflicting explanations for the mistake, all treated as the real reason. Among them: this was intentional, and is intended to show the scarecrow is in fact as dim as always this was intentional, because the filmmakers thought the word isosceles sounded "smarter" this was mistake on the part of the actor, and the script said "right triangle." this was a mistake on the part of the filmmakers Is there any firm evidence or statements from those involved about which explanation is correct?
